A towering wall of new storm-clouds rolls across the old red desert, the first true weather this world has known, trailing curtains of rain.
The first rain falls on the red rock in silver sheets, pooling in the dust, steam rising where it meets the warm bare stone.
A green processing-aurora ripples across the thickening sky, the visible signature of the new atmosphere being woven overhead in shifting curtains.
A double rainbow arcs over the new lakes, colors almost too vivid, the ice-melt water still clouded with the pale silt of newborn shores.
Lightning flickers deep inside the bruised purple of a thickening atmosphere, silent at this distance, stitching the clouds together with white thread.
The dust-haze that has hung over this world for a thousand years is thinning now, and behind it something extraordinary: a strip of actual blue.
A razor-sharp line cuts across the sky, one half storm-black, the other blazing clear, the weather front holding its edge like something newly invented.
The first snow falls on the new mountains, soft and tentative, dusting the raw rock in white, the peaks claiming their first winter.
Golden dawn breaks through fresh cloud in long cathedral shafts, the new atmosphere catching the light and scattering it in colors the old world never had.
A tornado of seeded cloud spins down from the processing layer, dark and deliberate, wringing rain from manufactured sky onto the waiting desert below.
Mist rolls off the new inland seas at sunrise, slow and thick as breath, drifting inland across the red plains in long pale rivers.
Hail hammers the bare basalt in a white fury, the stones bouncing and piling in the cracks, the first ice this lowland has ever received.
A second sun-dog hangs beside the real one in a halo of refracted ice crystals, the atmosphere dense enough now to conjure such strange optics.
Thunderheads build in stacked anvil columns fifty kilometers high, lit from within by their own lightning, a cathedral of new weather assembling itself.
The morning fog lifts slowly off the crater lakes, revealing water so still it mirrors the processing-aurora still fading in the brightening sky above.
A squall line sweeps the equatorial plains, visible from orbit as a bright white seam racing across the red-brown face of the waking world.
Virga trails from the cloud base in long grey brushstrokes but evaporates before reaching the ground, the air still too dry to accept the gift.
The first overcast sky, total and grey and low, pressing down on the new valleys, the world learning what it means to not see the stars.
A waterspout rises from the shallow new sea, white and spinning, the young ocean already wild enough to throw its own weather back at the clouds.
Sunset burns through forty kilometers of fresh atmosphere in shades of amber and deep violet that no instrument had ever recorded on this world before.
Ice-fog fills the highland plateau to the brim, level and white as a frozen sea, only the tallest new peaks breaking the surface like islands.
The first sandstorm meets the first rainstorm on the open plain, and between them hangs a curtain of dark mud-rain, the old world fighting the new.
A glory shines in the cloud below the ridge, a perfect circular rainbow surrounding the shadow of the terraforming station on the mist, precise and eerie.
Snow-squalls race across the new tundra in grey veils, the wind scattering the flakes horizontal, the first blizzard writing itself in white across the brown land.
The sky clears completely after the long storm, and for one held moment the new world stands under open blue from horizon to horizon, washed clean.
